body.text: That is the probing question for Session 2. It runs through the whole session: the grappling class, rolling and recovery, and the lesson.

body.label: Where this sits
body.text: Session 2 of 36. The Descent, Week 1, Arrival. On the mat that stage runs The Roads.
Both players stand and tie up. One arm over, one arm under.
The win is one thing: connect your hands anywhere on your partner's body. No takedowns, no slamming. Stay light and standing.

content.text: You are learning to make a connection the other person has to answer, which is the first thing that happens when you meet a stranger on the mat.

slides.title: How you win it
slides.question: In the Overhook–Underhook game, what counts as the win?

options.text: Connecting your hands anywhere on your partner's body
options.feedback: Anywhere. That's the whole win condition.
No takedowns in this one. Light and standing the whole time.
That's a different game. Here it's one over, one under, and the win is connecting your hands.

slides.correctText: One over, one under, hands connected. Nothing else scores.
slides.incorrectText: Read the note under your choice, then try again.

slides.title: What had to be true first

body.text: Every session is built around one key condition — the one thing that has to be true before anything else gets built.

body.label: Session 2 key condition
body.text: A connection the partner has to answer.
Not a connection they can ignore. Once you tie up, they have to do something about it. That is what makes it contact and not just standing near someone.

reveals.label: Still true every session: the tap

content.text: Any of the three ends the round immediately. When your partner taps, you stop. Not after you finish the move. Immediately.

slides.title: First contact
slides.question: Why does the tie-up count as real contact?

options.text: Because your partner has to answer it
options.feedback: Once you're connected, they have to do something about it. That's the key condition for today.
Nothing scores until your hands connect — and even then it's a game, not a match.

options.text: Because it's the strongest grip in grappling
options.feedback: It isn't about strength. It's about making a connection the other person can't ignore.

slides.correctText: A connection the partner has to answer. That's the condition the whole game is built on.
slides.incorrectText: Read the note under your choice, then try again.
slides.revealText: The right answer is marked above, with the reason.

body.text: In today's rolling you worked with people who still barely know you.
When you met a new partner, what did you do first? Did you go hard to prove something, hang back to stay safe, or joke to cut the tension?

body.label: Not a test
body.text: None of those is the wrong one. This is noticing, not grading.
How you make first contact on the mat — cautious, rushed, stiff — is your entrance.
Naming how you show up when nobody knows you yet is the same pattern, seen off the mat.

content.text: That entrance on the mat is the same one you use everywhere new. First day somewhere. A room full of people you don't know. Anywhere you're unknown.
Session 1 asked what safety is. This one asks what you actually do when you're new — the face you lead with when nobody knows you.

slides.title: So what did you do?

body.text: Think back to the first partner you tied up with today.

slides.question: When you met them, what did you do first?

options.sub: Came in strong, showed them something.
Stayed careful until you knew what you were dealing with.

body.text: That's it. That's the thing this session was after.
Going hard, hanging back, joking — all three are entrances. None of them is the wrong one. You've used yours plenty of times before today; the only new part is that you can see it now.

body.label: One question to sit with
body.text: Does that match how you want people to meet you?
Most people don't notice. That's what makes it a default.
It runs on its own, which is exactly why it's worth catching. Next session you'll have another new partner and another chance to watch yourself do it.

body.label: Nothing owed
body.text: Passing on this is fine. Presence is participation.

slides.title: Your answer
slides.prompt: How do you show up when nobody here knows you yet?
slides.hint: One word or one line is plenty. Loud, quiet, funny, invisible — whatever it actually is. Nobody is grading this and nobody else sees it.

body.text: Plain words. No need to make it sound good.

slides.title: The one thing from today
slides.question: What was today's session actually asking you to do?

options.text: Notice how you show up when you're new, and name it without judging it
options.feedback: That's the whole task. Notice it, name it plainly, leave the verdict out of it.

options.text: Fix the way you come across to people
options.feedback: Not yet, and maybe not ever. This session is about seeing the pattern, not changing it.

options.text: Work out whether your entrance is a good one or a bad one
options.feedback: No. A plain observation counts as a win here. It's data, not a verdict.

options.text: Win the tie-up against a stranger
options.feedback: That was the game, not the point. The game was there to show you the pattern.

slides.correctText: Notice it. Name it plainly. No judging.
slides.incorrectText: Read the note under your choice and try again.
slides.revealText: The answer is marked above. Notice it, name it, don't judge it.

body.text: Next session's question: What are you like before you trust the room?
Everybody has an entrance, and now you can see yours. Next time closes out Week 1.
That's the eLearning for Session 2.
